subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO QUALITY OF FOOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 20 I told the member for York West (Mr. Hamilton) that I would look into the provision of food for militia units at camp Niagara-on-the-Lake. This matter has now been looked into and,

as so often is the case, the allegations made have been found to be somewhat exaggerated.
However, the commanding officer of the camp who conducted the investigation has reported that the quality of catering, which was by contract, was not as good as it should have been when the camp opened. It should be pointed out that to organize a catering service to take care of a large number of men at one time and quickly does present some difficulties, particularly at the opening of the camp season before the catering organization has got into its stride. However, there has been steady improvement in the situation at this camp and the quality of food and arrangements for its serving are now reported to be reasonably good.
Since the difficulty here stems from the early camp catering period I am asking the army authorities to look into ways and means of getting the quality of catering up to better levels at the outset of militia camp training next year. Our objective is to provide members of the militia with first quality food well prepared and well served. I am hopeful that our studies of the situation at this camp and elsewhere will lead to improvements in the quality of commercial catering services for which we must contract to supplement our regular army facilities.

speechtext: Last evening we were discussing the matter of the administration of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the matter of old age pensions. The minister seemed to be rather pleased that I should keep this item open. I should like to tell him that the members of the C.C.F. party in this house historically have been acting as a goad and a spur to the governments of this country in the matter of old age pensions ever since the party was elected to this house. It was largely through the efforts of one of the original members of this party that the old age pension was established.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Oh!

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I see that a lot of other members agree with me. Today we have some 745,000 pensioners in Canada, and the cost to the Canadian government is about $353 million. I think that the fact that we pay that amount of money and are taking care of those people is all to the good in Canada, and we can be proud of the record. However, there is something very seriously wrong with the pension that is given out today. I think the Canadian people will support an increase in that pension because it is the actions of the present government at Ottawa that have brought about a condition that these people are not living as senior citizens of this country should live.
I refer to the fact that the $40 a month that is now paid to old age pensioners, to people in Canada when they reach the age of 70, is not sufficient for them to live in the way they should live after reaching that age. A few years ago, a pension of $40 per month probably would have been sufficient to take care of the needs of an average person, but the cost of living-the cost of rental, clothing, food and particularly medical attention in hospitals-has increased so tremendously that the value of the $40 per month is practically wiped out. The people are still trying to exist on a niggardly, paltry $40 which will buy very little. I do not know any place in Canada where a person can obtain decent shelter for $20 per month, certainly not in the cities. To try to exist on the remaining $20 a month, to buy food, clothing, medical care and medicine, with the costs today constantly increasing, means that these people just do not get them.

The government that sits opposite today is responsible for the increased cost of living. When they took the price controls off, immediately after the war, they allowed the cost of living to skyrocket to a point where they have found it necessary to see that the Canadian people got some increase in their income. Members of parliament increased their pay to $10,000 per year. Cabinet members increased their pay. Wage earners have found it necessary to go on strike to get more money in order to be able to cope with the constantly increasing costs of living. The provincial governments have difficulty in administering their own departments. The minister's estimates and the report of his department show how the costs of administering that department are constantly increasing because of the cost of living.
One group of people who seem to be unable to pass on their costs are the old age pensioners. Left with a miserable $40 a month, life to them is a mere existence. It is fortunate that in some provinces these people receive a little extra because the provincial governments have assumed a responsibility which I maintain is not theirs out of pity for the old age pensioners. The province of Saskatchewan, and also the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta, pay a supplementary allowance in order to help the pensioners to eke out an existence because they cannot exist on $40 a month.
The provincial government of Saskatchewan has assumed the responsibility for all medical care for old age pensioners. What a relief that must be for the people who live in that province compared with other provinces where the old age pensioner must spend part of his $40 a month on hospital care, doctors and medicines. Our province provides free medical attention, free hospitalization, eye, ear, nose and throat care, dental care and other assistance of that kind to needy pensioners without cost.

That is right. I was using the minister's words. I can remember your cherubic figure in those days, and I suggest that if you had gone on the old age pensioners' diet at that time you would not have had to go on an artificial one to attain your present fine figure. The minister's waistline in those days would scarcely have been appropriate for a minister handing out $40 a month to old age pensioners living in the condition of starvation in which they have to live. The point I am trying to make is this. The fact is that the situation is so bad that provincial governments have to enter the field in order to relieve the dire need of people who are unable to help themselves, whose earning capacity is practically gone and who have no [DOT]way of passing on increases in the costs of 'living to anyone else, as the manufacturers can. Even with the supply of food that we have in this country, old age pensioners who are attempting to live on this amount of money cannot help but be actually hungry. Coming from the prairie provinces as I do, and seeing the abundance of food in that part of the country, in my opinion it is a shame that these old age pensioners have to pay the prices that they do, even for the bread they get, for the meat they have to buy and the other things they have to purchase. The fact that people over 70 years of age are hungry in this land, with hundreds of millions of bushels of surplus wheat, is a tragic situation, in my opinion.
I believe that the federal government has got to assume responsibility for a larger and larger share of the payments to old age pensioners in this country. These people have made their contribution to Canada. They have completed their life's work and in their declining years most of them, through no fault of their own, find themselves in dire circumstances. They could live on $40 a month if the cost of living were not so high. But where there are cases of need, particularly in the matter of hospitalization and medical care, surely it is the responsibility of the federal government to see that their senior


citizens in any part of Canada do not suffer. If the provincial governments are going to undertake this, and they do it because the federal government refuses to do so, that is a sign that the need is there. It is a sign that the federal government should accept its responsibility. So long as these conditions exist we cannot be complacent; we cannot be satisfied and we cannot be proud of the achievements of the minister's department.
I am willing to pay tribute to what he has done in some fields. In view of the fact the cost of living is so high, with the resulting hardship on old age pensioners, I say that here is a place where humanity demands that the Canadian people should take care of their senior citizens. Some years ago when I came to this house I protested against conditions amongst the native people of this country, our Indians, particularly in the matter of health and welfare. I want to commend this department for the job it is doing in taking over the matter of health amongst the Indians. The result has been, as departmental records show, that with the new treatment for tuberculosis remarkable steps have been taken. It is only because we constantly bring these matters to the attention of the people of Canada so they know what is going on that we get action. I want to tell the minister that we are going to continue to pound at this government for action on the matter of old age pensions. Until we can get some action, we will continue to talk on every possible occasion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

I have just one or two
words which I want to say to the minister with regard to the level of old age pensions today. No one can deny that the level is such that many of our old age pensioners find themselves in an impossible position. The reason for it, of course, is simply this. While Canada has in circulation more and more dollars, those dollars buy less and less. Indeed, having regard to the remarks yesterday by the chairman of the Bank of Canada, we are facing inflation in this country. More and more the level of prices is rising as inflationary influences are felt. I regret that today little or nothing has been done by the government but to continue their course.
I believe we have arrived at a plateau and that prices will continue to rise rather than return to the levels of 1949, the basic year now taken as a standard by the bureau of statistics. The old age pensioners, because of that fact, find themselves in difficulties and in an intolerable position. My hon. friend mentioned that the entire responsibility is that of the federal government. I do not belong to that school. I believe that the provinces have a responsibility, without in any way relieving the federal government of

a primary responsibility which it has accepted to assure that old age pensioners shall not be made to suffer unnecessarily. The fact remains that there is also the responsibility of provincial governments.
I am not going to enter into a controversy that has been carried on between the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek and the hon. member for Yorkton, but it is a fact that in Saskatchewan the numbers receiving the maximum amount of the provincial government additional assistance to old age pensions is less than 30 pensioners.

I am going to be so brief and so succinct that I am sure my hon. friend will have no objection to my taking a few moments on the general item instead of discussing it piecemeal here and there. I am referring to the Disabled Persons Act, passed by this house in 1954. This act provides for dominion and provincial contributions; it provides for the payment of an allowance to those who are totally and permanently disabled as prescribed by the regulations. In my experience, this act is being altogether too rigidly administered. The joker in the act is the section that provides

Supply-Health and Welfare that the definition of total and permanent disablement shall be that definition determined by regulations.
The situation today, in whatever cases have come to my attention, indicates that the basis of interpretation excludes many persons who should be qualified and who should receive the allowance. I am not going into particular cases, but I am going to say this. The regulations were apparently designed to deny many persons who should be entitled. I have a recent example in mind, and I am not going to refer to the man's name because the minister has it. It is the case of a young man willing and able to work who is afflicted with a disease.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have that case.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
He has always been
willing to work, but he is stricken with a disease that has made him permanently the occupant of a wheel chair. He is a married man with one child. He does not ask for charitable assistance. I heard of his case and the difficult position in which he finds himself. I took it up with the authorities. The man has tried to train himself through the instrumentality of courses that are available to those who are totally incapacitated. Since he is a married man with one child he finds it difficult to take the type of training that is only available some 150 miles from the place where he lives.
The man's wife has endeavoured to work. From time to time she has been incapacitated, or at least ill, and unable to carry on. The definition of total and permanent disablement has denied him this allowance. This is one case of many. I feel that at the next session this question should be submitted to a committee in order to determine a fair and proper definition of total and permanent disablement. Parliament never intended that the definition should exclude many who should be entitled on the basis of the ordinary meaning of the words and expression "total and permanent disablement". I also feel that this is a matter that deserves the attention of a committee of this house for the reason that while in part the contribution is provincial and the definition of total and permanent disablement has been arrived at as a result of conferences with the provinces, there can be no justification for the rigid and utterly inexcusably restrictive nature of the interpretation of this term as now exists. In saying that, I realize that the provinces have an equal responsibility to make sure that the definition will guard
[Mr. Diefenbaker.!
against the possibility of claims being favourably accepted from those who should not be entitled but at the same time will be so interpreted that worthy cases will receive a fair opportunity to receive the allowance which is admirable in its purpose and deserving in its concept.
I have nothing more to say at this time regarding this matter, but I ask the minister to give consideration to having a definition arrived at in keeping with the ideas of this house when it passed the legislation. This is one of the great dangers of regulations. Parliament passes the law, regulations define it and, in many cases, the actual ambit of the law, and in that definition departs from the concepts that were in the minds of legislators when they gave support to the legislation in question.

That means in effect that a married man and his wife who are both in receipt of old age pensions and can prove under a means test that they are in need will receive a combined payment of $20 from the province of Saskatchewan. I do not say that to belittle the efforts being made by Saskatchewan. Possibly that province is doing all it feels it can do.

Under item 252 there is a question I should like to ask the minister.


He will recall that a few weeks ago I asked him a question on orders of the .day concerning news reports having to do with radioactivity. The particular reference in the news reports was as to whether or not persons in various occupations or persons being exposed to X-rays in trying on their new shoes and so on are getting too much radioactivity. As I recall, he indicated at the time that the matter was being looked into. Has he any further information on this point?

I am grateful to the hon. gentleman for asking this question because I had wanted at some time to make a statement on this subject. I would think it is possibly one of the most important matters facing the world and certainly facing Canada at this time. The minister of health in the United Kingdom recently made a comprehensive statement in the House of Commons. I understand that my opposite number in the United States is about to do so and I know that the same will be done again in the United Kingdom. In view of this, and particularly in view of my own participation recently in certain phases of disarmament activities, I feel that I should make a statement, and that I now propose to do.
On April 4, 1955, I tabled replies in answer to a series of questions by the hon. member for York-Scarborough which outlined in some detail the work being carried out by the Department of National Health and Welfare and other federal agencies in studying the health effects of ionizing radiation and in supervising the safe use of radioactive materials in industry, medicine and research. In describing the potential health hazards of radiation, reference was made not only to the deleterious effects on exposed individuals, but to the possible genetic damage that might be done by ionizing radiation arising from test explosions of atomic and nuclear weapons and from other sources of radioactivity. Anyone who has seen the statement made by Dr. Lapp, the eminent American scientist, will recognize that perhaps no subject that has been discussed in this house is as important as the one now involved in this statement.
Two important scientific reports have recently stimulated increased public interest in this matter. I refer to the report of the national academy of sciences in the United States and the report of Great Britain's medical research council which was recently presented to the United Kingdom parliament at the request of Prime Minister Eden. These two reports have confirmed the views expressed to me by the late Dr. A. J. Cipriani early in 1955 which largely formed the basis on which we have developed our own departmental program in this field. Dr. Cipriani

died after having served only a few months on the United Nation's special scientific committee, and Canada and the world owe to this late distinguished and eminent scientist a debt of gratitude which I am sure history will recognize.
I want to make it perfectly clear, speaking on behalf of the government, that if, as a minister of health, the expert technical advice available to me indicated that there were serious health hazards to the human race in the continuance of test explosions at the present rate I would consider it my duty to recommend urgent negotiations directed towards their total abandonment and thorough re-assessment of the international political consequences of such action.
Now, I must say at once that this is a complex problem, and one about which much remains to be learned in so far as the health effects of radiation are concerned. However, there is already a body of scientific opinion of very great value available to us. It is on the basis of this evidence, admittedly imperfect and at times contradictory, that we must base our decisions in this matter. The urgency for filling the gaps in our existing knowledge in this field was recognized last November at the United Nations when approval was given to a proposal put forward by the United States for the establishment of a scientific committee on the effects of atomic radiation, to collect and collate all available data in this field.
Now, this committee has made a valuable contribution. The place of Dr. Cipriani has been taken by Dr. E. A. Watkinson, who is responsible for our department's very considerable program of research in this field. On this committee will depend much of the scientific assessment in this very important field for the future.
In examining the health effects of radiation, two points must be borne in mind. First, the effects of radiation are almost invariably harmful. This characteristic is utilized to advantage in the treatment of malignant tumours by radiotherapy. Second, radiation is not a new phenomenon. Human populations have always been exposed to ionizing radiation from natural sources including cosmic rays from outer space and radiations emitted by compounds of certain heavy elements such as uranium and radium. It is therefore the degree and not the nature of the hazard that is new.
Now, in the past 60 years since the discovery of radium and X-rays, some individuals have been exposed to greater amounts of radiation than naturally occur in the everyday environment. As new applications of atomic energy to industrial, medical and
Supply-Health and Welfare research uses are discovered and developed; more and more people will be exposed to increased levels of radiation. This is altogether apart from test explosions or the possibility of nuclear warfare. The potential risks of deleterious effects to health must be weighed against the unquestioned benefits to be gained from the use of ionizing radiation in various forms and the exploitation of nuclear energy for constructive and peaceful purposes.
Now, before dealing with the health effects of test explosions, I should like to touch briefly on the hazards associated with these other uses of radioactive materials and to describe some of the steps taken by the Department of National Health and Welfare to ensure that high standards of protection against radiation injury are observed. In doing this I am answering a request made the other day by the Canadian Medical Association for a statement by the government on this subject.
As long ago as 1950, the department established a radiation service for the express purpose of providing health supervision over the use of artificially produced isotopes in industry, research and medicine. Among other things, this service includes advice to prospective users of radioactive isotopes on recommended methods of planning laboratories; periodic inspections of such establishments to ensure continued safe handling practices; the maintenance of a film monitoring service for measuring both gamma rays and X-rays, thus assisting in the protection of persons who may be exposed to these rays in the course of their work; guidance in regard to the safe storage of radioactive materials, as well as the safe disposal of radioactive waste. As a major contribution to protection efforts, we have also assisted in the preparation of a summary of the recommendations of the international commissionti on radiological protection for wide distribution to radiation workers throughout Canada.
As part of its advisory service, the department has also drawn attention to the health hazards associated with the use of shoe-fitting fluoroscopes. In this particular, I am answering directly one of the questions asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. In an effort to ensure protection for the customer as well as the members of the sales staff, detailed recommendations on the operation of these devices have been prepared and are being widely distributed. While it is acknowledged that this is not a major source of radiation, these machines contribute unnecessarily to the total radiation background. In this connection, the international

Supply-Health and Welfare commission on radiological protection has recommended that their use should be limited to strictly medical procedures under the supervision of qualified persons. This is a matter which the federal government has no constitutional authority to act upon and is one that has been brought to the attention of the provincial governments concerned for enforcement purposes.
Then, services for the monitoring of dental and hospital X-ray installations have also been made available through our radiation service for several years. A pamphlet was prepared on the subject of protection in diagnostic X-ray departments in response to an increasing interest in this subject from radiologists and X-ray technicians. In addition, the department provides advice in regard to the health supervision of cobalt 60 beam therapy units, which of course is a very important instrument in the treatment of cancer, and other similar sealed sources of radiation for the treatment of cancer and allied conditions. This may be taken then as an indication that Canadian physicians have been aware for some time of the potential hazards related to medical uses of X-rays and are developing methods to ensure the maximum safety against possible deleterious effects associated with the use of this very valuable diagnostic and therapeutic agent.
Recognizing, therefore, the public health implications of exposure to increasing levels of radiation resulting from the wider development of peaceful applications of nuclear energy the department, over a year ago, convened a meeting of experts to assist in planning studies and investigations which would enlarge our knowledge of this exceedingly complex field. As a result of the recommendations of this advisory committee, a special laboratory was established to determine levels of radioactive strontium 90 in certain food products and other biological materials. Our findings from these investigations will serve to establish a base line for the future. In addition to laboratory investigations, we are also developing studies related to the incidence of radiation-induced diseases and the possible genetic effects.
With regard to the latter, the genetic effects, the department is now engaged in investigating three distinct lines of research. The first is the assessment of trends in the genetic components of the public health. That is to say, a study of vital statistics records to determine whether there has been any increase in the incidence of certain conditions that might be induced by exposure to radiation. The second is a study of the incidence of congenital defects among offspring of heavily irradiated individuals. The

third is the measurement of spontaneous mutation rates for particular human genes. All we have to do is observe what happened to those Japanese fishermen to realize that there is, perhaps, no study as important to the human race as this one.
So far, we have been giving most attention to the first of these, which may give information on long-term genetic effects of ionizing radiation. Our country, with its well developed and highly mechanized and centralized system of vital records and statistics, is particularly well equipped to consider this approach. Should this prove practicable, it may lead to the extension of present health record and reporting systems to include a recognition of the genetic aspects essential to the assessment of this potential hazard.
It will be seen, therefore, that vigorous measures are being taken by the department to supervise, from a health standpoint, the use of all radioactive materials and to further research into the potential future hazards. The results of our Canadian research are being made available to the special United Nations committee to which I have already referred.
I come now to the question of the bomb tests and their implications for the health of this and future generations. As we see this problem, the chief hazards for world populations are of two distinct kinds:	(a)
those associated with the ingestion of radioactive material, principally radioactive strontium 90; (b) those associated with effects on reproductive tissues and having a possible genetic effect on future generations.
When a nuclear bomb explodes radioactive fission products are produced. Close to the site of the explosion, the radiation given off from the bomb and the resulting fission products can cause serious radiation injury and even death. For this reason, testing sites for these explosions have been chosen in remote areas. Some of the fission products are carried high into the atmosphere and eventually fall on all parts of the world. The potential hazard for humans associated with that portion of the fission products carried up into the higher atmosphere results from the fall-out of these products onto the surface of the earth.
Some of us may conceive the hazard of radioactive fall-out as an immediate danger to human health and well-being. This, however, is not the case and, for a proper understanding, it should be appreciated that the important radioactive element, strontium 90, slowly settles to the earth over many years and becomes incorporated into soil and subsequently absorbed into certain plants.

Since strontium is deposited chiefly in the bone, where a sufficiently high concentration could cause tumours or other serious effects, the consumption ol food with a high content of radioactive strontium could constitute a major health hazard. I now quote from the British report:
Such measurements as have been made of strontium 90 in human bone suggests that the highest levels are at present about a thousand times less than is considered permissible for those occupationally exposed.
Work which has been done to date in our country indicates that Canadian levels are substantially the same as those in the United Kingdom and in the United States. Nevertheless, it should be pointed out that the best scientific opinion suggests that for the population at large the concentration of radioactive strontium should not exceed one-tenth of that permitted to the small number of persons employed in radioactive industries.
With regard to the genetic effects, it is accepted that exposure of the reproductive tissues to ionizing radiation may result in mutations which are mainly deleterious in effect when transmitted to succeeding generations. However, according to the best scientific evidence available to this government and to the governments of the United Kingdom and of the United States, and from recent discussions that I had in New York with France, the testing which has occurred to date will have no significant effect on the genetic quality of the population as a whole. Therefore, the principal cause for concern at this time is not, as some have feared, the possibility of genetic damage that would adversely affect future generations, but what are called the somatic or the direct effects from radioactive strontium 90. It should be clear from what I have said that the present levels of strontium 90 are well within acceptable limits for the general population.
May I just briefly summarize what I have been saying before I take my seat? Three propositions have been arrived at after a most careful study of the British and the United States reports, and data available from other countries as well as from the findings of our own research. I may say the statement which I have given to the committee today represents the compilation and efforts not only of officials of my own department but of some of the most eminent medical scientists, chemists and physicists in our own country and some with whom we have collaborated elsewhere, so that I am giving a statement that has behind it the authority of the best skills available in this field. My summary, therefore, is, there have been no significant harmful effects on the world population as a whole from all the
Supply-Health and Welfare nuclear weapon tests that have occurred to date. If testing continues at the present rate the genetic effects on the world population will be negligible. However, the strontium 90 levels will increase and may ultimately reach a point beyond which harmful effects could result. I therefore suggest to the committee that this is evidence of the interest and concern which we share with other countries, in this important matter, one which is receiving our continuing study.

-while at the same time pointing out to him that the almost unanimous opinion of the report of Admiral Strauss on the ability to now control fall-out has been described by almost every observer in Washington by the charitable word "disingenuous" which is, of course, a polite term for a harsher expression.
I was rather interested to find that the Minister of National Health and Welfare was able to extract so much comfort and assurance from the report of the British medical research council recently tabled in the British House of Commons because from the information I have received direct from London, and in one case from one who is

actually engaged in research work tor the British medical research council, and from the reports on that report that were carried in the New York Times of June 13, I doubt whether the minister's optimism can really be justified. In this report in the London Times reference is made to the report of this committee of the medical research council as follows:
On the question of long-term genetic effects, the report states that present knowledge does not justify the naming of any specific figure as a limit for the average dose of radiation which might be received by the population as a whole. "It is highly desirable," the committee state, "that such a figure should be named as soon as possible; and we understand that the international commission on radiological protection has this matter under consideration."
"In the meantime, we feel bound to state our opinion that it is unlikely that any authoritative recommendation will name a figure for permissible radiation dose to the whole population, additional to that received from the natural background, which is more than twice that of the general value for natural background radiation." The recommended figure might be appreciably less, and those concerned with the development and use of such sources of radiation would be well advised to keep this possibility in mind.
Although no specific recommendations on longterm genetic effects are thus made, the view was expressed yesterday in circles closely in touch with the report that the effects of thermonuclear explosions would exceed the criterion in respect of radioactive strontium in bone at an earlier stage than they would approach any reasonable limits that might be recommended in respect of the total radiation dose to the whole population.
I suggest that that indicates that this committee has in fact been warning the world of the possible, in fact the probable dangers of continued thermonuclear tests. To pretend that we can get comfort from that and go on gaily approving such tests is I think a distortion of the facts. I have here an article written by Dr. James G. Foulks, department of pharmacology, University of British Columbia, in which he quotes leading British and United States scientists on this point. He quotes Dr. A. H. Sturtevant, one of the United States foremost geneticists, as follows:
There is no possible escape from the conclusion that the bombs already exploded will ultimately result in the production of numerous defective individuals, if the human species itself survives for many generations, and every new bomb exploded will result in an increase in this ultimate harvest of defective individuals.
Dr. Foulks also quotes Dr. H. A. Muller, who received the Nobel prize for his researches in this particular field. I would remind the committee that Dr. Muller was the man who was prevented from going to the Geneva conference by the United States atomic energy commission because of his
Supply-Health and Welfare views with regard to the possible genetic effects of thermonuclear explosions. Dr. Muller had this to say:
Despite a number of unfortunate publicized statements by non-geneticists casting doubt on the mutagenic effectiveness of small doses of radiation, the work has gone so far as to make it inconceivable, on physico-chemical grounds, for a single ionization track traversing a cell nucleus to be without its proportionate probability of inducing a gene mutation.
The article continues:
Actually, Dr. Muller believes it probable that a single ionization or molecular activation, when properly situated, will suffice to produce a mutation.
And again:
Such considerations have led one scientist to conclude that "the long-range genetic danger of exposure of mankind as a whole to low-level, but widespread and persistent radioactivity, is the most ominous of all the dangers of the atomic age."
The chairman of the subcommittee of the British medical research council is Sir John Cockcroft, usually considered to be one of the outstanding British scientists. I was interested in finding in Nature, volume 176 of July 16, 1955 a criticism of Sir John Cockcroft's estimate of the dangers of radioactivity by J. B. S. Haldane, usually considered one of the world's leading biologists. In the course of this article in Nature, Dr. Haldane suggests that Sir John Cockcroft's estimates of permissible dose may be ten times too high. I am not going to read the whole article because it is much too technical but the conclusion he reaches is that Sir John Cockcroft has been far too optimistic. He winds up in this way:
The problem is not insoluble. The figures given above could, I think, be improved. I have, however, deliberately used estimates made before the question of the genetic effects of experimental explosions was raised. Estimates made later may have been influenced by conscious or unconscious political or ethical bias. Research on this problem requires extremely careful planning, including the realization that apparently hopeful projects may prove useless.
I would point out further that as a result of this report by the subcommittee of the British medical research council last week in the British House of Commons Sir Anthony Eden agreed that his government would make direct approaches to the Soviet union, and presumably to the United States, with a view to seeking a limitation of these bomb tests. I would suggest that that was a more rational and realistic result of reading the report of the British medical research council than the one indicated to us this morning by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

255.	Administration of the Food and Drugs and the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Acts, $1,389,761.

Mr. Chairman, earlier today it was suggested that the discussion I had in mind might better be brought up under this heading. I refer to a question which I asked the minister following up one presented to him on May 24 and having to do with the toxic effect of colouring used on oranges imported from Florida in the United States. This question and the question of added colouring to foods may not seem too important, but when one considers the number of boxes of oranges that come into this country and the fact that it has been found that certain coal tar colours are toxic and poisonous, then I think it does become important. I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Vancouver Sun to indicate just how important this really is. This is an Associated Press Dispatch from Washington under date of July 16, 1956, and it reads:
Probers claim some food dyes ''poisonous", linked to cancer.
A special committee says there is evidence some coal and tar dyes used in food, cosmetics and drugs actually are poisonous or cause cancer.
The committee added that it may take the food and drug administration another 25 years to determine whether 116 dyes now certified as safe under U.S. law really are harmless.
It said the research program should be strengthened.
Only 15 of the 116 dyes certified under the 1938 food, drug and cosmetic act have been studied to any great extent, the committee said. These 15 are used in foods.
Just commenting on that article, I wonder if the minister could indicate to us how many such dyes are used in Canada in comparison with the number used in the United States. The article continues:
Among the 15 coal tar derivatives which have been studied, the committee said, 10 resulted in some harmful effects on experimental animals.
"Several are distinctly toxic (poisonous) when fed to rats at levels as low as one-quarter of one per cent of a standard diet," the committee said.
This morning the minister, in reply to my question, suggested that he was having the question of added colour put under the Food and Drugs Act for administration purposes. I was wondering exactly what his departmental findings were in respect to this substance that was used and what work has been done in discovering the dangers that are pointed out in this article, whether or not the colours used in oranges are the only food colourings that are being examined or whether we have used in this country food colourings from this coal tar substance. The article goes on to say:
The committee also said the practice of labelling certain dyes as harmless is unrealistic unless the amount which can be safely used is specified.


I should like to know whether we have any control of the amount of colour that is being used in those oranges, what the percentage is, and what experiments have been conducted to indicate that there is no poisonous effect.
The group concluded, in view of the widespread use of coal tar dyes in foods, cosmetics and drugs, that it could "see no alternative to strengthening of the present research position of the food and drug administration in the area of coal tar colours."
The question in my mind is whether or not the very fact that oranges and such foods are being put under the Food and Drugs Act is a sufficiently strong measure in so far as periodic examination is concerned, and exactly what the department has found in respect to the toxic effect of these colours, as mentioned in this United States dispatch.

There is one matter I should like to raise under this vote. I shall admit quite honestly that I am hesitant in raising it, and yet I have to. I am a great cheese eater. I like cheese. I like Canadian cheese. Nine times out of ten when I order dessert, I ask for cheese. Therefore I am very much interested in that product, especially if produced in Canada. I was very much disturbed at something that appeared in the daily press relative to the conditions in some of the cheese factories in Canada. I have been in receipt over the past few weeks of a great many letters from my constituents enclosing copies of what was published in the British Columbia press of an article under an Ottawa dateline. In almost all the letters I received, they pointed out that they felt, along with others, that they would be very much disturbed if the situation as outlined were not denied nor a statement made in public by the minister that the situation had been corrected.
It is solely because of my desire to see more Canadian cheese consumed that I agree with those who have written to me that, in view of the publicity that was given, now is the time to have some publicity counteracting it-as I hope-to the effect that the situation now is not as outlined in the press release, as the result of the investigations of Dr. Thatcher, the head of the department's microbiology section and the two bacteriologists in the same department who were with him. I am not going to place on the record the published results of their findings, because I am certain the minister knows to what I refer and the reason why I am so concerned about it. Can he give some assurance to this house that, as a result of the investigation, action has been taken and that those who like eating Canadian cheese can now do so without any

fear that the situation which the department found to be prevalent is now continuing.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I can give my hon. friend-and I am glad he raised this question-full assurance in that particular. Under the Food and Drugs Act, the dominion analyst advises me that our examination of Canadian cheese shows that it contains the qualities that justify all of us in this house ascribing to Canadian cheese the highest standard which we have attributed to it. My hon. friend refers to a paper that was written three years ago in reference to a particular batch of cheese. That paper must not in any way be construed as in any way a reflection upon the wholesomeness and the good quality of Canadian cheese, a liking for which I share with the hon. gentleman.
Is the minister referring to the same report? This says that 137 factories were examined.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is right.

Would the minister also point out that the situation was rectified shortly after the first investigation, which was three or four years ago, and that this was a repetition-which was very unfortunate, I might say-of an article written three or four years previously as a result of an investigation, of some three or four years previously, and it was repeated after the situation had been fully rectified?

I point out to my hon. friend that I am trying to do him a favour, if he represents a cheese producing area. It has appeared on the front pages of the Vancouver press. I asked whether or not this could be confirmed and whether the matter had been straightened out, and I did so in the interests of the cheese producers, because this has appeared in the press in recent weeks.

I think that the publication in the press of a report three years old has done a great deal of damage to the cheese industry. The fact is that the situation has been corrected, and there should be a statement to the Canadian people, as the minister said, that Canadian cheese is of high quality. I consider it most unfortunate that this report of three years ago concerning a certain number of factories has been given to the public and that a slap in the face has been given to the cheese industry of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I fully agree with what the hon. member has said, that this report should never have been published. It was done without my knowledge. It was with regard to particular situations. We all know that Canadian cheese can compete in quality with cheese of any country in the world.
Supply-Health and Welfare
The minister did not answer any of my questions. Perhaps he does not care to.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Yes, I was going to deal with them right now. I thank my hon. friend for acceding to the request, as he did so kindly, to discuss this matter under this item and not under the general item this morning. I shall simply say, in addition to what I have already said, that in taking the step that we did with regard to the particular colour in oranges the ban applies as of August 1. It was not because we had found dangerous levels in colour in oranges in Canada but because we simply wanted to take a precautionary step.
In the regulations under the Food and Drugs Act, provision was made for the use of 17 coal tar colours in foods. In addition there is a requirement that the maximum amount of colour to be used in any food is limited to one part per 3,500 parts of food or approximately 0-03 per cent. In surveys which have been conducted in the food and drug laboratories of our department, it has been found that this level is reached in only a few foods, and the level of colour in the majority of foods, where it is used, varies from one to two parts per 100,000 parts of food. At the time the permitted list of coal tar colours was established, and with the evidence then available as to the safety of their use in foods, no indication of harmful effects was evident. Moreover, no reports have come to the attention of the food and drug directorate that the ingestion of foods containing any of the colours in amounts permitted in Canada has caused harmful effects in humans. However, my hon. friend may be assured that this matter will continue to receive the attention of our officials in the food and drug division in conjunction with our own work along with that particularly carried on in the United States.

It seems rather obvious that the report referred to by the hon. member who spoke was more or less suppressed. I should like to ask the minister if that report was suppressed and why the information has only come to light now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: What report is that?
The condition that the hon. member has spoken about.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We have passed that item. However, I will answer briefly provided we do not carry on a discussion. We have passed that item.
Oh, no.

No, you have not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Well, there is no sense arguing. Our officials examine these things. Dr. Thatcher had made an examination of a particular group of cheeses. I would not want to be regarded as publicly criticizing an official who generally does great service to the country, but in this particular instance his report should not have been published. I was not aware that it had been published, I can assure my hon. friend, but that is the situation and what I said about Canadian cheese stands.

That raises an issue that I think is of prime importance. The minister says that it should not have been published. Is the minister saying that this information which has the character of dynamite should not have been published and made available?

On a point of order, that is not proper information. The minister has just made the statement that the report should never have been published. I want to say that the report was published at the time. The minister has just given information which is not correct. The report was published at the time and that was three or four years ago. It should never have been republished. If it has been republished now it should not have been done. The report was published. The information was never stifled. The information was given to the public at the time and these situations have been corrected since. It is not fair that the matter should be brought up again after an interval of three or four years.

You are making it worse all the time.

Indians and Eskimos health services-
257.	Operation and maintenance, $15,983,621.

The minister received a letter from the council of the Six Nations Indian reservation some time ago, as a matter of fact it was in April, regarding the situation existing there now at the Willingdon hospital on the reservation. I received a copy of the letter the minister received. I wrote to the director of Indian health services and subsequently received a letter from the minister explaining the situation. However, the minister did not answer one of the questions I asked him. I asked him if there had been a change of policy with regard to Indian health services at the Lady Willingdon hospital, and if so, when the change took place and why it took place.

It has always been the understanding of all the people on the reservation at Brantford that hospitalization was provided to them free of charge. It has always been the case up until very recently. During the last year, in most cases, although possibly not all, charges have been made and several bills have been sent out to people on the reservation after hospitalization has taken place.
It is my understanding, and I have it on very good authority, that subsequent to the sending out of bills for hospitalization some official of the department was sent to the Six Nations reservation after the minister received the letter to which I have referred and that some of these people at least were told that they did not need to pay the bill and that, moreover, they should forget ever having received a bill.
If the situation is as expressed in the letter to the minister and if after some complaints are made some people are told not to pay the bills they have received and to try to forget they ever received them, then I suggest to the minister that is a very unfair practice.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Was it an official of the department who said that?

Supposedly, yes. Either the people on the Six Nations reserve are to be charged for hospitalization or they are not to be charged. No charge has ever been made before. Therefore, I ask the minister now, as I asked in the letter I wrote to him in May, when that policy was changed and why it was changed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My hon. friend may be assured that th,e policy in this particular has never changed. The policy always has been that those who can pay should pay. That is the only policy. If there are hardships, my hon. friend might bring them to my attention. Of course, only a small portion of the Indians are able to pay, but where they can I think it is generally felt that they should pay. I am going to look again at the particular case to which my hon. friend refers to see what it is about. However, if the individual cannot pay, then of course he is not going to be called upon to do something he cannot do.

That is not the point. I do suggest that might be the case for Indians living on the reservations, living there permanently. There are, however, cases of Indians residing on the reservation and working off the reservation, only coming back week-ends or something like that. Then, there may be some excuse, but if the rule is to be made for one then it should apply
Supply

Health and Welfare to all. Where a person has been frugal during his lifetime and has saved his money, he should not be jeopardized in his old age or jeopardize his children by having that money taken away from them, while the chap who has not saved any money is getting away free.

I might mention the same
subject to the minister. I would ask the minister to look into the situation in British Columbia. I have letters in my files, I am sorry I have not them here, from the north Thompson tribes who complain about the fact that it was their understanding they were supposed to be supplied with medical attention while they were on the reservation. They complain that they cannot get a doctor to go to the reservation. They are told to go into his office, and if they go into his office he makes a charge. That is a complaint almost identical with that of my hon. friend, and it is from the north Thompson tribes in British Columbia.

Certainly, I will look into
that.

May I ask the minister now
a question as to what contribution is made by his department to the province of Saskatchewan for Indians who are in receipt of hospital care or are outpatients there?

In the case of Saskatchewan, we suggested to the government the desirability of including Indians under their hospital insurance scheme. We would, of course, be prepared to pay the premiums. The commission there was not able to accede to our request. We had been able to make similar arrangements under the hospital insurance plan in British Columbia. That being the case we continue to exercise towards the Indians in the province of Saskatchewan the same attitude that we do towards the Indians throughout Canada, and that is to pay their actual costs of medical and hospital care.

My question was based on
an article I have here quoting Mr. Bentley, the health minister. I should like to read it to clarify my question. Speaking about the health services rendered to Indians, Mr. Bentley had this to say:
Another difficulty, as Mr. Bentley saw it. was the problem of Indians In the program.
He is speaking about the Saskatchewan government health program.
The province had never been given any authority or responsibility for the health of its Indian population. That was a federal prerogative. But, under the federal proposal, the province must provide hospital and outpatient service for Indians.
I was wondering what the proposition was.

Supply-Health and Welfare
We do that now.

What was the proposition
which the department made to Saskatchewan in that respect?

I think I indicated that we
had offered to pay the premium cost of Indians under the hospital insurance plan in Saskatchewan. They did not want to include them.

There is one phase of the
medical health service for Indians that I should like to draw to the attention of the minister, and that is the field nursing service. There is a very fine body of women doing that work under a terrific handicap. For instance, there are no roads on the reservation. As soon as one leaves the main highway to go into the reservation, one is met by mudholes or snowbanks in the wintertime. These nurses are running the danger of losing their lives by freezing to death. I am wondering if the minister could not get together with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to do something about roads.
Last summer I went into several Indian reservations. When I came to one reservation I asked an Indian if he would take me around the reservation and he said, yes. We had not gone 100 yards until we came to a big mudhole. I looked at it and I said, "We will never get through that." He said, "Oh, yes, the nurse was here this morning and she went through; if she got through, you can get through too." The rest of the reservation was just a continuation of the mudhole. I do not think it is fair to ask these girls to take such chances by driving where there are no roads, either winter or summer. I think it would be a good thing if the minister would consult with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and try to get roads provided so that these girls, who are doing such a fine job, will have some chance of doing their work without taking their lives in their hands.

On this item, I should like to pursue the point raised by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand a moment ago. There is an attempt being made to encourage Indians to emancipate themselves from the reservation. There has been an increasing number doing so, leaving the reservation and finding employment in various capacities. As a result of this new move, I have discovered a few of them running foul of the regulations pertaining to Indian health services. Can the minister say if there is any formula which can be applied to those Indians who are not completely enfranchised, but who have moved off the reservation-perhaps they

might be working in a neighbouring military camp-and who find they have incurred medical expenses? They are presented with a hospital bill of $200 or $300 and this scares them back to the reservation. It is discouraging this very desirable movement away from the reserve system. Is there any formula being applied to ease the problem during the transition period?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes, we allow them 12 months. If they establish a residence off the reservation, after a period of 12 months they are expected to bear their own expenses. But we give them that 12 months in which to work it out. If they return to the reserve, as sometimes they do, the status quo is reverted to.
Is there any suggestion in the formula that the expense is borne only by those Indians who are actually paying municipal taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: There is nothing of that nature.

If they are not able to pay their own medical expenses, it means the municipalities automatically become responsible, and it seems to me that tying it up to some tax paying responsibility might be a step in the right direction.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Once they have established their residence, after a period of 12 months they are like anyone else. Most municipalities recognize that.

I should like to ask the minister if he has any answer to the problem I raised with him a month ago regarding the hospital at Selkirk supplying services to treaty Indians. I sent the minister the bill. I know that other arrangements have been made since and they are sent to the Dynevor hospital, but when is the bill going to be paid to the hospital at Selkirk?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: After my hon. friend asked his question I got hold of the director and he has sent out a message to get further elucidation. I hope that next week I will have something I can tell my hon. friend definitely.
I wonder if the minister would give me the number of doctors in attendance at the Willingdon hospital at Ohsweken?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: There are four.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that up until the time Dr. Davis retired, he looked after the hospital alone. He made thousands and thousands of calls all over the reservation himself.
There were two doctors with him, I think.

For a good many years there were not two doctors; he was there alone. Now with tour doctors there the doctors refuse to come out after six p.m. to make a house call in the reservation unless it is a case of very extreme emergency. How is a person going to know at six p.m. at night whether or not the case is going to develop into an emergency at midnight? I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that with four doctors doing the work that we will say two did before-I am not criticizing, actually I am criticizing because I do not think they are taking the interest in the job they should take if they refuse to make the calls after six p.m. Probably their hours are short enough, and they could quite nicely make emergency calls after six p.m.

I shall certainly look into that, but I want to pay this tribute to the doctors and nurses in this service. If my hon. friend knew the difficulty of getting professional help, because of the incomes received outside by professional people, he would see why I am anxious to pay a tribute to them. We have part-time doctors, full-time doctors and nurses all through this country who are giving yeoman service in remote places as well as in settled areas, and while that does not excuse an individual indiscretion or failure of duty, my tribute to them all is certainly well deserved. I shall be glad to look into the other question and discuss it further with my hon. friend.
The reservation at Brantford is not in a remote place. The doctors do not have to travel over bad roads.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I said I will be glad to look into that particular situation.

I accept that, Mr. Chairman, but I do want to point out that Ohsweken is not comparable with other places. What salaries do these doctors get there? Are they underpaid in comparison with other doctors? Is it a fact that they are underpaid in comparison with what they could earn in private practice? I do not know whether it is at all comparable or not. As I understand it, these doctors are not Canadian-born, and they might not be able to get positions that other doctors can get.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Two of them are not Canadian-born, but that does not alter the fact that they are all good doctors.

I know it does not. I do not want to be misunderstood at all. Can the minister give the salaries of these doctors again?
Supply-Health and Welfare
The minister paid a tribute to the doctors and nurses in the service. How well is he paying the doctors? What is the average salary of the doctors?
I asked that question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The average is $7,500.
The average is $7,500? That does not answer my question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is the question I was asked.
What are the four doctors getting?

Would my hon. friend not think it would be fair if I gave him that information privately? I have given the average. I do not think it is fair to give the salary of an individual, but I shall be glad to give it to him.

In the minister's explanation he mentioned the Saskatchewan health service and said that he had offered the province the premium which has been $40 a year. He knows as well as I do that that does not in any way cover the cost of hospitalization.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I said we would continue the tubercular care, as we had in the past. I was simply putting it that way. We wanted the Indians to be included in the hospital insurance plan to the extent that the plan covered the ordinary individual. We would continue to be responsible as we are now.

Yes. Since the minister's
department and the department of Indian affairs accept Indians as wards of this government, I certainly cannot understand how the minister can reconcile his explanation with the position that he has taken with respect to this offer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I do not think there is any difficulty. The situation is briefly this. There is no legal responsibility on any jurisdiction in Canada to look after the health of the native population of this country. That is the general situation; but the federal government has assumed that responsibility. Ten years ago our budget for Indian health was a little over $1 million. Today, it is between $18 million and $19 million. Hon. members, like the hon. member for Brandon and the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand and others, who have Indian hospitals in their constituencies, recognize the great service that is being performed by our officials under the direction of the present director in the matter of the improvement of the health of Indians and Eskimos throughout this country. All one has to do is to look at the

Supply-Health and Welfare reduction in the incidence of tuberculosis as a result of this program in which we operate hospitals all over the country at considerable expense for a population of around 150,000 people. The fact that the Indian population began increasing almost concurrently with the establishment of this nation-wide hospital policy is a pretty good indication of the effectiveness of this work.
There is no attempt on the part of the government of Canada to get out of its responsibilities. In the particular case to which my hon. friend has drawn attention we are simply seeking for general hospital purposes, with the payment of a premium, to do the job in a more efficient way, and we could not get agreement in that particular. In British Columbia we were able to have it included under the hospital insurance scheme there; that is all. It does not mean that there has been any retrogression.

The minister will remember that some time ago I brought to his attention some of the problems faced by the administrators of the hospital at Abbotsford, British Columbia, in their dealings with the Indians. One of the problems was the fact that in many instances Indian children were brought to the hospital, or hospitalized, and because of the nomadic character of their parents, when the children were ready to be discharged the parents could not be located, and therefore the hospital had to accept the responsibility of caring for those children until such time as the parents could be found, even though they were eligible for discharge prior to that time. I did raise the question. I realize, of course, the province of British Columbia has assumed responsibility for the Indians-at least they are bringing them under the hospital plan. I should like to ask a further question on this Indian problem. A moment ago the minister mentioned the incidence of

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say just a few additional words concerning the federal government's proposals to the provinces regarding hospitalization insurance.
The minister was perfectly correct last night, even though he quoted just excerpts from the remarks I had made in the committee on estimates, in putting statements of mine on the record to the effect that this group hopes the proposals the government has made will soon be put into effect. We express that hope and we give the minister our support to that effect, despite our clearly expressed dissatisfaction in that we feel these proposals do not go far enough.
We feel that in this year, 1956, we should be a lot closer to an over-all program of national health insurance. The minister knows that that is our view, and that even after we get any beginning such as he may be able to bring before parliament after obtaining an agreement with the provinces we will press for an improvement and a moving on to an over-all national health plan including provision for all of the costs of health care, and including as well sickness benefits to take the place of income lost when the breadwinner is out of work.
Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, having made a speech last night expressing our general aim in this field, I shall content myself now with a few remarks with respect to the actual proposals the government has made to the provinces.
I say quite frankly that our concern is that time is running on. The minister may say it is only a few months since the proposals were made to the provinces. It is actually six months since that time, and with the Liberals months have a way of running into years, years have a way of running into decades and decades have a way of running into lifetimes. We are afraid that unless some bold steps are soon taken by the government the proposals that were made last January may collect dust along with the green book proposals of 1945, the draft bill of 1944, the Marsh report of 1943, a few speeches from the throne in the early forties, and the Liberal platform of 1919.
In six months three provinces have signified their readiness to come into the plan outlined by the federal government in January, and I think credit is owing to those three provinces, British Columbia, Alberta

Supply-Health and Welfare and Saskatchewan, for the studies they made of the proposals and for the replies they gave to the minister. But surely it must be evident that with this much time going by and no other province showing any indication that it is going to come into the plan, the time has come for the government to revise its proposals.
There are certain modifications which might have the effect-in fact we believe they would have the effect-of encouraging the provinces that have not yet agreed to come into the plan to give the plan favourable consideration. I will not rehash the arguments we had in committee and those which took place last night between the hon. member for Mackenzie and the minister with respect to the inclusion of patients in tuberculosis and mental institutions, but that is one way in which the plan could be modified with the possible result that more of the provinces might agree to it.
I think perhaps an even more significant modification could be made with respect to the sharing formula. I will not take the trouble to spell out in detail this roughly 50-50 formula that is based on a 25-25 proposition. As I said in the committee on estimates, we feel there is justification for splitting that federal portion into two divisions, one arrived at on the basis of the provincial per capita cost and the other arrived at on the basis of the national per capita cost; but we think that instead of a 25-25 proposition it should be a 37J-37J proposition, or something even better.
In stating that view we are concerned not only with setting out these proposals in a way that will make a better appeal to the provinces, but we are also concerned with the end result. Despite what was said yesterday by the new Liberal member across the way, an attempt should be made to put the payments for medical and health care on the basis of ability to pay rather than according to the illness that hits the particular individual. To the extent that payment for hospital insurance or health insurance or medical care is left to the individual or even to direct premiums to that extent you are making people pay according to their requirements for health care rather than according to their ability to pay. To the extent that you pay for health care out of the federal treasury, which is collected in the main out of income tax, corporation tax and taxes paid to some extent at least according to ability to pay, you approach recognition of the principle we advocate, namely that health care should be paid for according to ability to Pay.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, both because in principle we think it is more correct and
TMr. Knowles.]
for the reason that we feel more of the provinces might come in if the percentage paid out of the federal treasury were increased, we think the government should give consideration to revising the 25-25 formula to a higher figure. I suggest that 37J-37J or indeed a still higher figure might be considered.
We feel something should be paid by the provinces in order to bring them into the picture, not only administratively but in terms of cognizance of the cost, but that the main burden of the care of the health of the Canadian people should be paid for out of the main treasury of the Canadian people, the federal treasury, which as I say is collected more than any other treasury in this country according to the ability of our people to pay.
Last evening the hon. member for Vancouver South, making a speech when the minister was trying to encourage us not to talk about health insurance on the administrative item but to wait until we got to this item, spent most of his time dealing with what he referred to as the lethargy of Premier Frost in not showing more interest in the proposals made by the federal government. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South, and I agree with the Minister of National Health and Welfare that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec hold a key position in relation to the formula the government has laid down. The formula is that six provinces, representing a majority of the Canadian people, must agree before it comes into effect, which means that one of the central provinces has to agree. If all the other eight agree and those two stay out, the terms of the formula have not been met.
Therefore there is no question but that there is particular importance attaching to the consideration which Premier Frost or Premier Duplessis may give to this matter. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South that anything that can be done, whether it is through a provocative speech such as that made by the hon. member for Vancouver South or through the co-operative attitude shown by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, to persuade those two premiers to give more serious attention to this matter is all to the good.
I should like to take just a moment to develop the question which I interjected during the speech last night by the hon. member for Vancouver South. That is, if the federal Liberal government is keen-I am satisfied the Minister of National Health and Welfare is keen, because I am sure that there are few things that would delight his heart more than to get this plan on the

statute books-about matters concerning health and welfare, I suggest that they should begin talking turkey or something stronger to the Liberal premiers of four of the provinces in this country. Premier Frost could very well reply to the hon. member for Vancouver South, "Supposing I do agree, that would bring the total number of provinces up to four but the plan still could not go into effect." Unless you get Quebec to come in-of course if you could get both Ontario and Quebec to come in that would be fine; that might be different-but if you cannot get both Quebec and Ontario, if you simply get Ontario along with British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan you would have to find two more.
Where are you going to find them? There are four Liberal provincial governments in the country, in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Manitoba. I suggest that if Liberals like the hon. member for Vancouver South and the Minister of National Health and Welfare want this plan to go ahead they should see to it that those four Liberal premiers realize the importance of their position in relation to this formula.
I noted the remarks the minister made with regard to Premier Frost; I have noted the very co-operative manner in which the minister has approached this whole question, but I suggest that the premiers of those other four Liberal provinces hold a pretty important place. I suggest to the minister that he would make much better headway if he would just get those Liberal premiers to take a good look at the matter. As I say, Premier Frost can say, "What does it matter if I come in or not; there would be only four provinces that agreed, Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan." If two of the Liberal provinces came in, two out of Manitoba, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, then there would be five, and only one more would be needed.
I suggest that one or the other of these two lines should be taken by the government if they mean business with respect to their own proposal. They should either revise the proposal with regard to the percentage the federal government is prepared to pay, or they should talk turkey to the Liberal provinces of this country so we can get somewhere with this formula which the federal government has laid down. I urge upon the government that one or the other if not both of those courses be followed. Although the plan may have shortcomings, which we deplore, nevertheless it would be a step in the right direction. It would be a beginning after all these years, 37 of them, during which the Liberals have been promising health insurance. I think it is high time we had at
Supply-Health and Welfare least a beginning along the lines laid down in the federal government's proposals to the provinces.
