264. To authorize and provide for general health grants to the provinces, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory upon the terms and in the amounts detailed in the estimates and under terms and conditions approved by the governor in council including authority, notwithstanding section 30 of the Financial Administration Act, to make commitments for the current year not to exceed a total amount of $48,460,401, $33,750,000.

Mr. Chairman, there are two matters I should like to place before the minister arising out of this vote. The first has to do with the possibility of help being given under these grants toward the construction of small hospitals. I understand that at the present time the requirements of the grants are such that it is practically impossible for a hospital with fewer than 30 beds to qualify for help.
We have made many grants to hospitals with fewer than 30 beds. There was one case in western Ontario where the hospital had only 9 beds.

This difficulty has arisen in British Columbia, and I believe it is due to the standards required under the regulations. In some small towns it is not necessary to have a hospital with all the facilities to be found in a city hospital.
Could my hon. friend give me the particulars of the case so I might see just what are the facts?

This case arose in Agassiz where the citizens were trying to work out a scheme for the construction of a small hospital, but evidently the requirements were such that it was impossible for them to qualify for assistance. Perhaps the minister would explain to the committee how these regulations work in a case of that kind. If a patient requires special treatment, he or she can of course go to the large hospitals in Vancouver or New Westminster or one of the other larger centres, and there is no need for a small hospital to have all the facilities that are found in the larger hospitals.
Is there not some way in which this help could be spread out to a greater degree to aid in the construction of hospitals in the small centres? The grants have been in existence for eight or nine years, and perhaps the time has come when there should be some concentration on helping with the construction of these smaller hospitals which would not have all the facilities of the main hospitals in the country.

Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
My hon. friend may be assured that there is no discrimination as between the small and the large hospitals. The procedure is simply this. The province is the only jurisdiction under the British North America Act that has authority over hospitalization, so if a province requests a grant for a particular hospital we are prepared to make a grant of $1,000 per acute bed or $1,500 for a chronic bed. The requirement we have is that of safety. We have had no difficulties. I can only recall one hospital, and I think it was in the constituency of one of the members opposite, where we had a difference with the hospital authorities, and there we were not satisfied that they had complied with the report of the fire marshal of the province. That is the only case I know of in British Columbia.
I have sent for the particulars of that case. I do not know what they are, but I can assure my hon. friend that no discrimination whatsoever was made between the large and small hospitals. The conditions are laid down primarily by the province. If they say that the hospital should be built there and assistance is forthcoming from them, then we give consideration as to whether or not in the circumstances there should be assistance given by the federal government. However, I am going to have that case looked up and I shall be very glad to discuss it with my hon. friend when I get the facts.

Does the minister have any
check made in respect of the decisions of the provincial governments about these smaller hospitals? It may be that in British Columbia the provincial government is laying down provision of such a nature that these small communities cannot qualify for this federal assistance. Perhaps it would be wise for the minister to look into that situation. I should like to have the minister's assurance that this plan is designed to help with the construction of hospitals in small centres as well as in large centres and, even though the hospital to be built in the small centre has not the same high standard of equipment as the hospital in the large centre-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I assure my hon. friend that is the case. I have already given him that assurance. The position and the standard of equipment in the hospital does not enter into our calculations at all. I am not aware of the particular facts; I shall have to go into that particular case. Ours is a sharing plan. The province must give at least a similar amount. There have been a number of cases in two provinces where the province has not wanted to give the full $1,000, and as a result we have had to give less than $1,000, or we were not able to give more than


$1,000, and the result was that the total amount of money available was not sufficient.
That may be the case; I do not know. I shall be glad to go into it, but I can assure my hon. friend that there is no discrimination under this plan. We have provided assistance, along with the provinces and with the voluntary groups, for the building of almost 80,000 hospital beds in the last eight years. I am sure that represents a tremendous achievement on the part, first of all, of the voluntary bodies, the provincial governments and ourselves. It is a cooperative arrangement, and is I think a great monument to what can be done co-operatively in this country.

The minister will realize that this is one of the serious problems facing the residents of the small communities, and I hope he will do his best to remedy the situation. The other question I wish to raise has to do with the program for research in connection with the rheumatic diseases, such as arthritis. Under the health grants there is no specific provision for this particular type of'service.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: There is no particularization at all for any research grant. We have given funds for arthritis research in great amounts for many projects, particularly in British Columbia, but the vote does not call for a particular research. The procedure is that we have a special committee that take into account all applications for research grants. This committee is made up of eminent officials in our own department and outside. If they say that a certain project should receive consideration and should receive financial assistance, that forms the basis for our policy. My hon. friend says there is no grant for research in rheumatism and arthritis, but he will find that we have given almost $491,000 for research in that particular field to date.

I did not say there was no money spent on research in our province. I said there is no specific grant for that particular type of research. There is provision for a general public health grant and a public health research grant, but research for arthritis could only come under either of those headings if the provincial government or the public health authorities should decide that research on arthritis is a matter of public health. I am asking the minister whether this disease is not serious enough in its effects on the Canadian people as a whole to have a health grant for the specific purpose of dealing with the problem of arthritis.

We have raised this question in other years, and the minister has said that money is spent on it, just as he started to say today. Last year he said in reply to questions, as reported on page 6296 of Hansard, that $78,000 had been made available to an arthritis and rheumatism society in British Columbia. I found out subsequently that that $78,000 covered a period of several years. It was not a grant for one year. It included amounts paid for seven or eight years, beginning with the year 1948, and out of that sum $67,000 was for the provision of equipment-
A travelling clinic.

-and not for research at all. Only $11,000 had been spent for research; not all of the $78,000. I am also told that the total research grant for rheumatic diseases in Canada, as of last summer, was $173,719.73 which would make an average annual grant of $21,715 for the dominion research program for rheumatic disease. That does not seem to be very much. That does not seem to go very far toward meeting the problem of research in connection with this particular type of disease. Can the minister tell us whether there is any plan at the present time for increasing this particular type of research, and if so, what it is?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I .thought I had explained the situation carefully earlier, but perhaps my hon. friend has understandably not appreciated the nature of the grants. If we were to have a research grant for arthritis or for rheumatism we would have to have equally a research grant for every conceivable disease.
Why does the minister say that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am going to explain. The general public health grant is the generic term that covers general public health which includes research, which includes treatment, which includes everything. Then the other grants are the tuberculosis control grant, the mental health research grant, the hospital construction grant, the cancer control grant-
Those are special grants under the plan.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Those are specific ones, but you could not possibly have a grant for every conceivable disease. Any particular disease in this country that is given priority by our scientific assessment committee or by decision of the government based upon other considerations can qualify for a research grant. Out of the national health program we have spent on research over $7 million since the beginning of the program.

How much of that was on arthritis?
Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Just a minute. When this program began there was no money spent at all on research by the federal government except through the national research council's grants, which were very limited. With regard to arthritis, the figure my hon. friend referred to in British Columbia of $78,496 was for mobile and other equipment. That did not have anything to do with research. The research in these things is done at places like the Connaught laboratories. It is done by the University of British Columbia medical school. It is done by the neurological institute of Montreal. It is done by the Charles Best research institute in Toronto, the Dr. Collip institute at the University of Western Ontario, the great research centres where personnel are heavily concentrated.
Taking arthritis, we had a project on ACTH and cortisone, as the hon. member for Lanark will know, that alone cost $436,000. That is only in the field of arthritis. We have other projects now. There is one at the University of Western Ontario. There is a small one at Laval University. There are two at McGill University. I am not sure whether or not there is one at the University of British Columbia. These are projects of research into the various forms of rheumatoid arthritis, but the organization to which we have given assistance in British Columbia is not a research body. It is a body to teach people what can be done, to bring them to the clinics. For instance, there are the automobiles they use. I do not know if my friend has seen those in British Columbia. Undoubtedly he has. They are very fine and they were provided largely, I think entirely, by us out of our funds. But these are not research projects.
My hon. friend may be sure that consideration is given to this subject, which is a very important one. We estimate that there are about 150,000 people in Canada who suffer in a serious way from rheumatoid arthritis of one kind or another, and I am told there are over two hundred different types. There are many more people who have the disease. The Metropolitan Insurance Company has made an estimate of 700,000 people who suffer from rheumatism in one form or another, not in the way the 150,000 do but who are afflicted by it.
These various research centres are dealing with this subject. But you have to have the personnel to do it, and you have to have the projects to do it. Last year under the national health grants we provided almost 2,000 different bursaries to 2,000 individuals engaged in the health fields, and of that 2,000 over 250 went to men engaged in fundamental research, cancer, rheumatoid arthritis, heart disease and various other maladies.

Supply-Health and Welfare
We are now about to make a big grant for the new heart disease institute in Montreal. We have just finished giving a grant of $150,000 to an organization in Toronto for the study of heart disease. My hon. friend will see that not only rheumatoid arthritis but all these various other diseases are the subjects of great research projects.

The minister has himself explained very clearly the very large numbers of Canadians who are suffering from this disease, and he knows just as well as I do just how serious a factor it is in the national picture. Surely those very facts are sufficient to warrant the extension of the health grants to cover arthritic and rheumatic diseases. The minister has a general public health grant, a tuberculosis control grant, a mental health grant, a venereal disease control grant, a crippled children grant, a professional training grant, a cancer control grant, a public health research grant, a laboratory and radiological services grant, a medical rehabilitation grant and a child and maternal health grant. These are all excellent. I am not quarreling for a moment with any of them, but does the minister not think that the problem of arthritis is sufficiently serious to warrant having a specific grant for the purpose of dealing with this condition?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I agree that it is an important matter, and it is the subject of research, as I have indicated to my hon. friend. I do say that if we were to particularize all the illnesses that should be the subject of research the list would be endless. I do say that rheumatoid arthritis is not the most important. One of the most important concerning which we are now engaged in a coordinated campaign effort is heart disease. Another is cancer.
You have a grant for cancer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I know, but we have not got one for heart disease.
Perhaps you should have.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I think my hon. friend misinterprets. Except for the tuberculosis and the mental health grants, these various grants are all generic in quality and out of any of these sums, general public health grant, research grant, cancer control grant, can come moneys for research in those particular fields. Out of the general public health grant can come, in addition to a research grant of $500,000, assistance for arthritis or anything else. My hon. friend is asking that we should name arthritis as opposed to other diseases. I cannot agree with that. It is very important and it is a very unfortunate malady, but the titles of these grants does not interfere with the nature of the assistance that is given.

I am only suggesting that if there were a grant for this purpose it would focus attention on the problem, and I think the result would be a great deal faster and more far-reaching action to solve that problem than we are likely to get under the present method of handling research in connection with arthritis and the other rheumatic diseases.

There are two points I would like to discuss under this vote. One has already been mentioned by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, the question of hospital construction grants. Back in 1948 the government laid down what was undoubtedly a very fine principle, namely the acceptance of responsibility in a financial way for a basic contribution to the construction of hospitals in this country. As was mentioned a little while ago by the minister, the basic grants as they were outlined back in 1948 were $1,000 per bed for active treatment hospitals, $1,500 per bed for chronic, convalescent, mental and tuberculosis hospitals, and $500 per bed for nurses' living quarters. I think the government should be commended for the fact that in the years that have gone by since 1948 they have extended that to include other fields. There is now some provision for a basic hospital construction grant in the realm of laboratories, health centres and training facilities. The government, as I say, are to be commended for the action they have taken in that regard.
I do think it is time for the government to take a second look at their basic construction grants. Since 1948 when they laid down the rates of $1,000 per active treatment bed, $1,500 for chronic and convalescent beds and $500 for nurses' beds, there has been a great alteration in the cost of construction throughout the dominion. I am speaking for no other province except British Columbia, and in British Columbia I only speak on behalf of Vancouver.
In 1948 when the basis was laid down, the cost of active treatment hospital construction, excluding equipment, was $9,000 to $10,000 per bed. There has been a great deal of construction going on in Vancouver in the realm of hospitals, and I am informed by the authorities there that the cost this year for active treatment hospitals is $14,650 per bed. When you compare that with the basic cost in 1948 of $9,000 per bed I say I think it is only reasonable that the time has come for the minister to give consideration to increasing the basic grant at least by an amount that is going to take up a fair share of that increased cost. I do not want to enlarge too much upon that point, having stated it.

In addition, in connection with this question of hospital construction grants, I do think the minister should pay particular attention to one aspect. When this principle was laid down in 1948, and when the chronic and convalescent basic rate was set at $500 higher than the active treatment rate, as I read the reports of the department they state very definitely they had a reason for doing that. One of the objectives of the hospital construction grant was to encourage the construction of additional accommodation for chronic and convalescent patients in order to remove these categories of patients from active treatment hospital beds. They can be accommodated in specially designed hospitals, or in wings attached to acute hospitals, with potential savings in nursing and other costs. I think it is regrettable that the objective of the government in 1948 has not been achieved.
I was most interested in reading a breakdown showing how the grants of the minister's department have been made. Since 1948 the grants have gone on this basis: for active treatment, $31,161,000; for chronic and convalescent, $5,037,000; mental hospitals, $14,293,000; T.B., $4,292,000; bassinets, $6,604; nurses beds, $8,574,000; community health centres, $4,142,000; combined laboratories, $130,000; training facilities, $35,000. These grants total $74,268,000. But the important point is this. The grants for active treatment have totalled $31,161,000 and for chronic and convalescent only $5,037,000. Although the government in 1948 recognized the problem by granting an additional $500 per bed if they would build convalescent hospitals, these figures show what has occurred.
Now, sir, during the last day or so we have heard about hospital insurance in Canada. This government will have to assume a substantial part of that cost. Therefore the government should be keenly interested in efficiency in the operation of hospitals and keenly interested in seeing that, although they pay all that is required for medical and hospital attention, they do not pay any more than they have to for these services. I think most medical men will agree that now, when we are moving into a national health insurance plan, we have to concentrate more intensely on convalescent hospitals. I am not speaking of the chronics, I mean those who require hospitalization but do not require the medical care of an acute hospital for a certain period of time.
Unfortunately this spring I had to spend 14 weeks in hospital and I know, as a result of my observations, that including myself, a number of the patients there did not need
Supply-Health and Welfare to be in an acute bed. Our requirements could have been met in a convalescent bed. I made inquiries of the hospital authorities in Vancouver, and they told me that the difference between the maintenance of an acute bed and a convalescent bed in Vancouver is the difference betwen $18 and $10 a day.
Now then, that being the case, if under proper arrangements and planning medical attention can be given the convalescent in the neighbourhood of the acute, so you could get that treatment if required, it does seem to me that in the interests of federal government financing they should not only increase the basic hospital construction grants in comparison with 1948, but there should be a greater increase in the grants for the construction of convalescent hospitals. This would act as a persuader to the provincial authorities to increase their activities in this field of hospitalization.
I have spoken to a great many medical men and hospital authorities, and they all seem to be in agreement with that opinion. I am certain the minister must be in agreement also. I do believe he should give a little more in the way of financial persuasion so as to get this work under way in all provinces. Admittedly it will require the expenditure of additional money, but I think it is almost axiomatic that sometimes you can save money over a long period of time by making an expenditure at the proper time. Surely it would not be asking too much, because under the item we are now discussing I note that the allocation is only $6,762,000' plus $2,736,000 of a revote; plus $4 million in another revote, or a total in all of $13,499,060' in hospital grants in this present fiscal year. I most certainly would like to hear the comment of the minister on those two aspects which come under this item.
There is one other subject which I mentioned in the general discussion and agreed to have stand over, and that is the question of the natural health resources of this country. I took occasion in the committee to speak of it, and on other occasions I have spoken at length on Canada's natural health resources. I am not going into the details. I only say that I am still convinced Canada has the greatest natural health resources in the world. If we had the proper research to develop them Canada, and in particular British Columbia, would become the health mecca of the world. We have a potential multi-million dollar industry, but so far we have not done anything about it. Last year the minister was kind enough to say he

Supply-Health and Welfare was interested. If we refer to page 6286 of Hansard for July 16, 1955, we find that I said this:
But I hope the minister who, I understand, is interested in what I have said, and has made some inquiries, will give some indication of his stand at the present time and tell us if something is going to be done in the next year or two, or in the next five years perhaps, in the matter of research and development.
Then the minister said:
My hon. friend may be sure of my deep interest. This matter is now being discussed, as a matter of fact, with the Charles Best institute ... in Toronto, and a project is possibly under way. In any event, the matter has been referred to the research committee and it is being given further attention.
In view of this statement by the minister last year about research and the Charles Best institute, would he kindly give us a report as to what has taken place in the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I am sure I express the view of every member in this house when I say that one is reminded, when the hon. member speaks, of the fact that he himself has unfortunately been indisposed for some months now and has been a sufferer in one of the Vancouver hospitals. Several months ago we told him how glad we were to see him back, and perhaps I would be permitted to do so again at this particular moment.
With regard to the other matter, it is one on which there is a divided opinion scientifically, as to whether or not there is value in that particular form of research. Last year I indicated my own personal interest in the matter, along with that of the hon. gentleman. We did discuss the matter with the director of the Charles Best institute, Dr. Best himself. Dr. Best felt that since at this particular moment he is engaged on a program of research he could not disturb it with advantage at this time, and quite properly so. The matter was discussed as well by me and by one of my officers with another research director who is now giving consideration as to whether or not his program of research in his centre-he has a very important cancer project under way-could be fitted into this particular field, because this one is not a specific subject. This is one, as my hon. friend knows from his interest in it, that covers a very wide field.
I can only say to him that the matter had not escaped my interest even before he raised it. I can assure him, as I think I did privately, of my own personal interest in the matter. These researches cannot be undertaken by us; they have to be undertaken by particular medical scientists. They have to be people who can fit into their program. I certainly hope that will be possible.

With regard to the hospital construction matter that my hon. friend raised earlier, our objective, when we brought in the national health program, was to assist in the building of 60,000 beds in a period of 10 years. We have exceeded that objective. I am not saying there is not much to do yet. Of course there is; there always will be in the field of health, but I think, as I said a moment ago, that the combined efforts of all of us, of all jurisdictions and of people generally in this field, have been notable in this country, and we have every reason to be proud. We estimate now there are about 25,000 beds to be built. That number will increase as the population increases. That represents pretty much the current need, but it does not create, in these terms, the problem that might be suggested by the mere mention of the 25,000.
I agree fully with what my hon. friend has said about chronic beds. The reason we have a higher grant for the chronic, as opposed to the acute, is in part the reason he himself mentioned a moment ago. We wanted to encourage the provinces; we wanted to encourage private institutions to pay more attention to chronic care and to building institutions for chronic keep, and we have not succeeded. When I say "we" I mean all of us. I have sought in declarations I have made from time to time to keep emphasizing the importance of chronic care. Of course one of the finest chronic hospitals in Canada is St. Mary's in London. I mention that to those who are interested in this work. If they will go there they will see what can be done in a chronic institution. I can only hope there will be an increasing interest in this phase of the matter.
My hon. friend said that one way to do it is to increase the amount. All I can say at this time is that that matter, of course, continues to receive our attention.
I should like to ask the minister a question. These general health grants to the provinces are matching grants?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Not all.
A lot of them are.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The hospital construction grant is; the cancer control grant is; the rehabilitation grant is in part; the laboratory and radiological services grant is in part; the venereal disease control grant is. All the rest are not.

What I would like to find out is this. A certain amount of money is available to each province each year, provided it can match the grants that have to be matched. Can the minister give us the amount of money that was available last year

to each province and how much of it was taken up? I think it will partly answer some of the questions.
It is a very long list. Does my hon. friend want me to table it, or does he want me to go through the whole list? It is quite an extensive table.
If the committee is agreeable, table it.

There are the general public health grants, which are not matching; there is the tuberculosis grant, which is not matching; there is the mental control grant, which is not matching; there is the research branch, which is not matching; and the professional training grant, which is not matching. The hospital construction grant is; the cancer control grant is; the child and maternal health grant is not; the rehabilitation grant is, in part. Therefore my hon. friend will see that over two-thirds of the money made available by the federal government to the provinces is not on a matching basis.
Obviously the money must not be given unless for good purposes. I am not criticizing
Supply-Health and Welfare the provinces for this, but sometimes for personnel and other reasons they have not accepted the moneys. For instance, I shall take my hon. friend's own province of Nova Scotia. The amount available to Nova Scotia last year was $2,480,581. We have approved projects in the amount of $2,041,000. There is a free balance left of $438,000. That is for Nova Scotia. If I file this table it might be of interest to my hon. friend.
That is fine.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: With the permission of the committee I will table it.
Could we have it in Hansard at this point?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes, it is going in now.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it agreed that the Minister of National Health and Welfare can include this table in Hansard at this point?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext: The minister said that $400,000 was available to Nova Scotia last year that was not paid out. Was that because of inability to match the grant?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No, it was not all matching. A portion of it was for hospital construction. Hospital construction was the largest amount, $183,000; $8,000 for crippled children; $4,000 for professional training; $35,000 for mental health; $3,000 for general public health, and so on.

Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding the legitimate differences of opinion members in different parts of the house may have on many problems, it is rather a satisfaction that we have now spent some hours today discussing those problems which concern human distress, and that no party and no individual in the house has any particular monopoly on compassion and regard for those problems. It is with some diffidence that a member who does not belong to the medical profession speaks on a subject with relatively little knowledge; but I want to add just a few words at this time which I think properly comes under this vote, Mr. Chairman. I refer to the matter of mental health.
The minister may recall that on the opening day of the session, and for some weeks, there stood in the name of the member for St. Lawrence-St. George a resolution to the effect that a national survey might be called under the leadership of his department, in co-operation with the provincial authorities anti other groups in Canada, with respect to the question of mental illness. Members here, who are all relatively well informed, need not be told about the problem of mental health in Canada at this time. We are all pretty well aware of a real interest in that aspect of illness.
I think we as Canadians might take some degree of legitimate pride in the fact that Canada stands somewhat in the forefront in what is being done in this field. It may be, Mr. Chairman, that while we are giving consideration to the question of mental health today we should not be too smug, because it is possible that throughout the country there may be little clusters of men like ourselves in mental institutions who are trying to decide what they should do with us here. It is a question of relativity and of degree. I am not at all certain, Mr. Chairman, that I would want to pass an intelligence test for admittance into this honourable chamber at this time of my life.
I think we are all seized with the importance of mental illness, and this is borne out by the fact that in a constituency such as I have the honour to represent we have one


of the great international institutions in this field, the Allan Memorial Institute presided over by one of the leading psychiatrists of the world, Dr. Ewen Cameron.
My proposition, Mr. Chairman, is one which I suggest requires no money from the government of Canada. Even within the vote the minister has under this item it may be that his department would give the necessary leadership in encouraging private institutions, provincial medical authorities and the professions themselves to make what I would call a reappraisal of the whole problem of mental illness. If that is done, and if additional money is required, then I am sure those great benefactors throughout Canada, both private and corporate, who are interested in this problem would gladly respond in providing whatever funds are necessary for this service.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, while the house has not been required to engage in a long debate on the resolution standing in my name, I thought it only right in the interests of all my fellow Canadians who are suffering from mental illness today and who have very few to serve as spokesmen for them, that all of us in this chamber and our friends and relatives who are more happily blessed should take a moment to suggest that notwithstanding the great work that is being done by provincial and federal authorities, by the profession itself and by helpful and compassionate individuals, we all might take a new look at the whole question of mental illness and make a national survey in order that this modern pestilence may soon be obliterated to the extent that we as decent people in our modern society might expect.

Mr. Chairman, I would like: to ask the minister a question with regard to the general health grants which are participated in by the provinces, and in particular a grant which has heretofore been made to St. Patrick's College under the mental health training project for psychiatric social work, which in 1954-55 amounted to $2,739 and in the preceding year to $2,600. It is my understanding that this project was approved by the Ontario department of health but was turned down by the federal authorities. The grant was used to pay part of the salaries of a lecturer in psychiatry and the professor of psychiatric social work. Would the minister say what reason there is for reducing what is a small grant in so far as the department is concerned but a very important one so far as the college is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
My hon. friend said it was approved by Ontario. That is not exactly

the case. If this grant was made available it would be made by the federal government on an application sent to us by the Ontario government. They are only the channel in that sense; they do not contribute anything.
I grant the minister's remarks. I had not intended to imply it was a 50-50 arrangement, but is it not true that the provinces ask for approval of these grants?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: They are passed on to us. We took the position that it was mainly a social work grant. We had given assistance before. It was a grant for work that had some element of mental health in it but it was basically for social work. We felt in fairness to other similar applications where there was a greater emphasis-I do not say a greater work but a greater emphasis-in this field we would have to give the matter consideration, as we did.
I hope the minister will reconsider, because as I understand it this will have a disrupting effect on the continuity of the service.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am very familiar with the situation.
I am sure the minister must be, but it has just come to my notice.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for mentioning it.
The minister will continue to consider the matter, will he?

I would just like to make a brief comment on the topic raised by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. On February 14 last I received an interesting return on the subject of mental health in Canada which indicates it is a problem, as was pointed out by the hon. member, that is of growing significance in Canada. For example, in the period from 1950 to 1954 there has been an increase in the total number of admissions of mentally ill patients to hospitals. In 1950 the figure was 16,411 and in 1954 the equivalent figure was 29,351.
It is very important, of course, that we provide institutional care for this type of illness, but coming to the next heading I think it brings us to an even more important approach to the solution of this problem. There is an active movement on the part of the laity to do something about this increasing problem. For example, the White Cross appreciate that the best solution to the difficulty is not necessarily within institutions, but rather it lies in trying to rehabilitate our mentally ill and emotionally ill within the framework of society itself.
Supply-Health and Welfare
Considerable progress has been made in encouraging volunteer interest in this important aspect of the problem. It seems to me, however, Mr. Chairman, that the laity needs some professional guidance, and that guidance must come mainly through the phychiatric social workers.
According to the information I received in this return it would appear we are somewhat deficient in the number of trained psychiatric social workers available in this country. In the year 1954, the last year for which figures are available, the total number of psychiatric social workers employed on a full-time basis right across Canada was 37. If one looks at the provinces one finds that Newfoundland has one, Prince Edward Island none, Nova Scotia two, New Brunswick four, Quebec 15, Ontario 10, Manitoba one, Saskatchewan two, Alberta two and British Columbia none.
That obviously is a very inadequate number to deal comprehensively with this volunteer approach to the subject. Could the minister inform the committee what steps are being taken to make available a greater supply of trained psychiatric social workers?
Before I resume my seat I should like to say to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George that I hope he will repeat his motion next year, so we may have a chance early in the session to have a comprehensive discussion of this matter.

Last year we trained 236. I want to say to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George that I am well aware, as I am sure the committee is, of his great interest in this matter long before he came here. I want to thank him for the great work he has done as a layman in connection with the Montreal mental health association. I can only say to him that the problem on which he has focussed our attention is an important one.
It is true that mental illness is one of our serious major problems, but not any more serious than it is in the United States and other countries. I would not want to make odious comparisons, but it is a fact that the number of people who are going into institutions is on the increase. That should not be taken necessarily as an indication of the deterioration of the human body in this country; it is largely an indication of the new techniques of diagnosis, the greater skills which are available and the type of institutional care that is provided.
I should like to emphasize that in seeking to do what we can do with the moneys provided by the federal government we must recognize that these are problems which engage the attention of the provincial departments of health, which have the primary

Supply-Health and Welfare responsibility. Our role is one of co-ordination and supplementary assistance.
We have sought to give emphasis to two things in this field. First is prevention and treatment. We now have in existence some 105 mental health clinics, whereas when this program began eight years ago there were only 15. The purpose of these clinics is to reach the mentally ill person before his illness takes on a maturity which justifies confinement. These clinics, together with the child guidance clinics we have established on a pilot basis in a number of centres, are proving most valuable in our program of prevention.
The second aspect to which we are seeking to give emphasis is in the field of research. My hon. friend has mentioned the Allan Memorial institute in Montreal, which is carrying on most important research work. We are giving grants to other places for this purpose as well. My hon. friend may be assured, as indeed the committee may be assured, of our great interest in this problem. I have always felt, and I feel and say now, that one of the ways in which we of the western world can demonstrate our capacity to provide a desirable form of society is by the interest we take not only in this particular matter but in all matters having to do with health.
I want to pay tribute to the voluntary organizations in this country for the work they have done in the field of mental health, and I want to pay a special tribute to the Salvation Army. I know some of the work they do, as does the hon. member for Bran-don-Souris, particularly in the city of Toronto. I repeat my tribute to them as well as to all religious bodies for the work that is being done.

Grants to health organizations-
265. Canadian mental health association, $10,000.

What procedure is followed in deciding whether a grant shall be made under this item? Is application made to the federal government, or does the province in which the organization is located make an application on its behalf?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: There is a variety of methods. Most of them come to see us personally, and where it is said to be a national organization we seek to establish whether in fact it is such. An organization may have a name which suggests it is national in scope when actually it is regional or even community in scope.
What criteria are used to decide whether an organization is national in character?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: If they carry on operations in all provinces or in a greater number of provinces.

Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: During the sittings of the committee on estimates several hon. members asked the minister if consideration was being given to increasing the grant to the Health League of Canada. I have not the record before me, but my recollection is that the minister gave one of those kindly answers in which he paid tribute to those carrying on this work. Has his kindliness reached the point where he will recommend an increase in this grant?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My hon. friend will appreciate that we get many requests and have only so much money. I can only say in regard to these grants, some of which are shown here and some of which are still under consideration, that they are matters that are considered in the department. When we come to prepare our estimates next year I shall be in a better position to give my hon. friend an answer. I can assure him of my great sympathy with the work of the Health League of Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to repeat at length the points I made when I spoke yesterday on the first item with respect to the amount paid to our old age pensioners. Neither is it my intention to get involved in the arguments which developed this morning when the supplementary payments made in the various provinces were being discussed. Rather I rise simply to remind the minister that in the view of an increasing number of Canadians it is the responsibility of the federal government to see to it that our Canadian senior citizens have a decent standard of living.
As far as I am concerned, it does not help the case of our senior citizens when hon. members suggest that part of this responsibility should be borne by the provinces. As I said yesterday, when you put any portion of this responsibility on the provinces you are calling for a reinstatement of the means test, at least to a certain extent. The only jurisdiction with sufficient resources to provide old age pensions on a universal basis for all Canadians as of right is the federal government.

Once again I urge the minister and the government to consider the needs of our people and in the light of the increased resources of this country do something at an early date to raise these pensions.
I suggest to the minister that it is not the part of wisdom for him to criticize and speak against those of us who urge an increase in the old age pension, because if he stays in his present position I am sure, as he is, that it will not be much longer until even he and even the government of which he is a member will have to do something about this important problem. There are rumours about a certain event in the political life of Canada which may take place on October 29 of this year or June 17 of next year or somewhere in between. 1

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Do you want me to tell you when?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I do not suppose that the Minister of National Health and Welfare really knows, any more than I do, the precise date for the election. These are the suggested dates: October 29, 1956, June 17, 1957, or some date in between, say in April or May of next year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We are bound to have an election within the next two years.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
And the chances are that it will be on Monday, since that is what is provided under the Canada Elections Act. I suggest that with a surplus developing in the federal treasury, with an increased gross national product, which means that at the present tax rate still more money will come in, and in view of the fact that with the easing of world tensions there is likely to be quite a substantial reduction in the national defence budget next year, there is quite a possibility that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will make headway with his colleague the Minister of Finance and get out of him money not only for health insurance but for an increase in the old age pension.
I suggest, therefore, that instead of criticizing those of us who advocate that an increase be made, he should take these appeals to heart and realize, as I am sure he must, that this government does not dare face the people of this country without doing something about this issue on which there is growing feeling. I urge with the least possible delay an increase in the old age pension.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
My hon. friend and many
others have spoken on this subject all through my estimates, and this is the first chance I have to make a reply which I think should be made from this side. My hon. friend referred to the Minister of Finance. He need not 67509-417
Supply-Health and Welfare seek to select one member of the government as against any other, because the fact is that every member of this government is as interested in these problems as any other member of this house, and the Minister of Finance is certainly as interested as is the hon. member.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is good.

With regard to old age security, we on this side of the house need not apologize for what we have done and are doing for the aged citizens of this country. We are now spending more for old age security than any other country in the world on a comparative basis. We are the only country that hqs a non-means test system. The other day the hon. member for Broadview mentioned the United States system, and I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would agree with me that he would not want to compare the project that came out of the old age security committee a few years ago with the kind of suggestion which was made by the hon. member for Broadview, when in fact the committee recommended against the particular suggestion the latter made.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In principle the minister's statement is correct, but not with respect to the amounts that are paid.

It should not be forgotten that this year alone we have increased our total commitments to the aged by some $11 to $12 million. Ninety-five per cent of the moneys that are paid for old age security and old age assistance in this country comes from the taxpayers of Canada, under policies proposed by this government in this house. That is the fact. I think the hon. member for Prince Albert pointed out this morning the desirability of making sure that we should recognize that the provinces have their responsibility in this particular as well as the federal government, and I think that is true. I recognize the validity of what my hon. friend said about trying to maintain the non-means test character; but at the same time, whilst we are giving consideration to these problems-I wish to say that the government's policy will be announced when the government is in a position to do so-I may say that nevertheless we should not overlook the fact that the federal government is not in any way dragging its feet in the provision it is making for the aged citizens of this country.
In Newfoundland the federal government provides $7,599,405; in Prince Edward Island, $3,313,000; Nova Scotia, $18,411,000; New Brunswick, $13,246,000; Quebec, $77,110,000; Ontario, $134,644,000; Manitoba, $21,953,000; Saskatchewan, $22,331,000; British Columbia,

Industrial Relations
$44,657,000; Alberta, $22,681,000. The whole cost of old age pensions three years ago in Canada was only $10 million more than the $77 million we are now paying to the province of Quebec, and it was not as great as what we are paying to the province of Ontario, $134 million. So anyone who says this government is not doing its duty to the aged is stating something not in harmony with the facts.
We have no reason to be ashamed on federal account of what we are doing for our senior citizens. I could not help feeling that it was unfair this morning-and I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will agree-when one of the hon. members sitting behind him referred to myself, heartless man that I was, because I would not recommend any increase for the aged of our country. I want to say to the hon. member, who is not in his seat, that I take second place to no man in this house for what I have sought to do for the aged of our country. Since I have been a member of the government we have made important modifications in the old age security program. We have increased the amount. We liberalized the income ceilings before we had the nonmeans test program, and we have conducted ourselves in a way that 1 think justifies my saying, with all those who sit to Mr. Speaker's right, that we do not need to hesitate at any time to face the people of this country for what we have done for the aged and for other sections of the people.
My hon. friend keeps mentioning elections. I assure him that in this particular matter we can hold our heads high, because no government anywhere in any part of the world has done so much as this government has done for the senior citizens of our country.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, June 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles for the second reading of Bill No. 211, to provide for annual holidays with pay for employees.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ANNUAL HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I had the honour of adjourning the debate the last time this matter was before the house. May I say I also have to be very careful because I remember that at one time earlier in the session when one of the hon. members opposite had two items standing in his name on the order

paper, I spoke on the wrong item. There was one on which I intended to support him and another on which I intended to oppose him, and as the house will remember I spoke on the wrong one.
I am in somewhat the same spot today, because with respect to one of the items standing in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) having to do with holidays I intend to oppose him, but as far as this particular bill is concerned, although I was taken by surprise last time and only entered the debate under the exhortation of my friend the hon. member for-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION OF ANNUAL HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Comox-Alberni.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ANNUAL HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
-Comox-Alberni	(Mr. Barnett), I have had some time to think about it in the meantime and I have decided that this bill is worthy of all the support I can give it.
I may say I have come to that conclusion after thinking over carefully not only both sides of the question but all sides of the question. Quite often I find my heart on the same side as a good many of the hon. gentlemen opposite but I often find my head on the other side, or perhaps I should say my pocketbook. Quite often I am thoroughly in agreement with a good many of the things they suggest, and we on this side are presenting them to our own cabinet ministers. We have to press for them both in public and in private and the argument we have to meet is well, where is the money going to come from? I think some of my hon. friends on the other side do not always have to meet that argument as we do.
Therefore we have to watch our step as to what we support, but I do think that in this case that consideration does not enter into the picture, because the question of public finances is not involved in Bill No. 211. I will state frankly, Mr. Speaker, that one of the things that would incline me to oppose the bill at first glance would be that it seems to me that this parliament or any other lawmaking body should never pass a law where what is to be covered has already been covered by the people in the ordinary course of their own actions.
I submit that if we examine the general situation with respect to holidays with pay in Canada we will find that by and large the people of Canada have solved their own problems very satisfactorily with regard to this matter. We also know that the bill applies only to the minority of workers in Canada who can be covered under our constitution by federal legislation, and that the vast majority of workers are covered by provincial legislation.

I find that six provinces already have legislation similar to that proposed here. They are Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. British Columbia and Saskatchewan have the best laws. Modesty prevents me from saying which is the absolute best, but Saskatchewan is not so very far behind.
I find that only 400,000 of Canada's total working force of more than 5 million could be affected in any way, even theoretically, by the bill proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I also find that of the 400,000 workers who could be theoretically affected by the bill, 93 per cent of them are, by and large, already covered fairly satisfactorily one way or another by arrangements which they have worked out themselves, either as the result of collective bargaining or through the ordinary business processes involved in the relationship between employer and employee.
The matter boils down to this, that only about 7 per cent of the workers who could theoretically be covered by federal legislation might get some real and immediate benefit under Bill No. 211, advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Therefore it seems to me that we have to ask ourselves what is the advantage of passing such a law if only a minority can be effected in any event and only a small fraction of that minority are already outside the limits of the benefits proposed in the bill.
After careful reflection I have come down on the side of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre with respect to this matter, because it does seem to me that the parliament of the Dominion of Canada has a moral obligation to set a good pace in all measures for human betterment, and I certainly do not think that in any matter involving wages, working conditions or that sort of thing it should ever be left to the national government of Canada to fall behind any of the provinces, even the most progressive provinces of Canada such as we have in the far west.
Therefore I have decided to lend whatever support I can to the passage of the bill. While I have no doubt that if the bill gets to the industrial relations committee we will be able to improve some of its details, by and large I think it is a good bill worthy of support, and I commend it to the consideration of the house.

When I first read this resolution my first reaction was one of a faint sort of hope, born no doubt of wishful thinking, that its scope might be broad enough to include members of parliament. But after I got down to a serious study of the bill, and read particularly the explanatory note as to its purpose, I could not help but think what a great pity it is that such legislation is even necessary, because we are all our brothers' keepers whether we are employers or employees, and certainly annual holidays are in the interests of both.
In the world in which we live today, annual holidays are a necessity for health and for efficiency, and because of that they are in the national interest. Furthermore, the economic cost of annual holidays to employees is more than recovered in the gains to industry through less absenteeism
on account of ill health and greater production on account of better efficiency. Not only that, but we are living in an age when our way of life is challenged, and we are proponents of a way of life which is primarily based on the importance of the individual.
All our democratic system and all our democratic institutions have been built up on that principle, and certainly in an age of ideological conflict we cannot afford to forget that even for one minute. But on the other hand, Mr. Speaker, as I reflect more deeply on the bill, I must come to the conclusion that in one sense it hurts our democratic system, because of necessity it removes responsibility from the individual and we cannot remove responsibility without at the same time removing freedom of choice. These two factors are absolutely essential for the preservation and the development of our democratic way of life.
The explanatory note says that the purpose of this bill is to provide that all employees in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction be granted at least two weeks' holidays with pay after one year of employment. Certainly the stipulation of paid holidays is also a necessity because in our high cost society that we have built up here in Canada few employees can afford holidays without pay, and few can save up enough to enjoy a really good vacation out of their savings.
I think the important thing to remember about this legislation is that the key to this problem is not the number of employees affected but the number of employers, because it rests with every employer to grant these concessions to his employees whether they ask for them or not. I know it is pretty well admitted that the majority of our employers throughout Canada have already granted holidays with pay and that, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver South, only a small percentage of employees of the total working force of Canada will benefit from this legislation, but I think proportionately the number of employers will be smaller still.
The point I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, is that this very small group of employers, by shirking their responsibility to care for their employees, are doing a great disservice to the cause of democracy, because it is their irresponsibility that has made this legislation necessary. I have always been grateful that I had the opportunity of taking my university training in the field of science, because an understanding of the great laws that govern the forces of nature help very much to understand the human forces that control society. One great natural law is the

Industrial Relations
balance of forces. All the great forces of nature are very neatly balanced, and I think the greatness of Shakespeare as a dramatist lies in the fact that he understood, perhaps more than any other writer of his day, how the internal forces inside of people are also very nicely balanced, and when that balance happens to be upset by a chance happening, or by some flaw in the human character, then these forces have to work themselves out until a new balance has been established. The working out of these forces can often lead to tragedy. It perhaps leads to tragedy more often than to the happy ending which we call comedy.
If a very small number of employers do not treat their employees properly the question naturally arises, why not? What forces are at work preventing their doing it? Are they forces of greed for more gain; are they forces of fear that industry cannot stand the extra cost; or are they purely economic forces which prevent their doing so? I think it is necessary to know, because the great challenge which the free world faces today has arisen from these human forces borne of a sense of injustice and a sense of neglect, which have come about primarily because capitalism failed to realize it is not enough for enterprise to be free. Besides being free enterprise must also be responsible.
I would like to see more emphasis on scientific training in our schools and particularly in our business colleges, because if employers had a better knowledge of the forces of nature I think they would also have a better understanding of how human forces work and of the consequences that would result from their actions.
I have made these observations, Mr. Speaker, because I find myself in a peculiar position with respect to this bill. As far as the principle is concerned no one can disagree with it at all, and I certainly give it my hearty support. On the other hand there is some doubt in my mind as to whether this is the best solution to this problem. As a parliament of Canada our aim should be to build up through the country a system of free and responsible enterprise. How can we ever develop responsible enterprise if government is continually going to intervene and take upon itself responsibility that more properly belongs to the individual? How much better it would be if every employer did the right thing, not because there is a law which compels him to do it but because it is the right thing to do. In those circumstances this type of legislation would not be necessary.
I would hope that the Minister of Labour might consider setting up somewhere in his department-perhaps he already has the

machinery with which to do it-some machinery to survey problems like this so we would know exactly how many employers are not treating their employees responsibly, and not only that but also the reasons they are not doing so. We should also have machinery established to assist them to do the right thing. If it is clearly a matter of management or efficiency, then it would be much more positive for us to have someone go into that business and give the necessary assistance in order to enable them to do the right thing merely because it is right.
It seems to me this age is labouring under two misconceptions. One of these is that human nature cannot change. There are hundreds of thousands of people in the world today who can prove that this conception is contrary to the fact. There is abundant evidence in every part of the world to prove that human nature can change and will change voluntarily much more quickly than under legislative compulsion.
The second great misconception is that present social evils will be cured by increased social justice, more education and a greater sharing of wealth even if it is done through compulsion. I am convinced the cure will not come in that way. We cannot obey all the laws we have now, and the only way this problem is really going to be solved is by finding the answer to our human weaknesses. Unless we do find the answer to our human weaknesses humanity will go from crisis to crisis until lawless dictatorship takes over.
Therefore I would suggest that whenever we deal with any social problem of this kind we should know exactly what it is with which we are dealing and all the pertinent information should be obtained. In this case we should know how many employers and employees are involved, and the reasons for their not employing methods which we consider today to be simple elementary social justice. I would like to see this legislation deferred until the Department of Labour has had an opportunity to make this survey and obtain this information, and until it has been able to give more thought to the question of finding a better solution than that presented by passing more legislation.
It seems to me that this type of legislation, which little by little encroaches on the freedom of the individual and limits more and more the freedom of choice, is in the end going to defeat its own purpose because as I see it the answer is responsible enterprise. This represents democracy applied to industry and to economics, and I fail to see how we will ever preserve democracy by curtailing freedom.

Mr. Speaker, if my counting is correct I believe that nine members of the house have spoken to the second reading of this bill. I am encouraged as I check over the positions taken by these nine members, in that seven have indicated they are in favour of the bill or at least that they support its principle. The eighth member, the hon. member who has just taken his seat, seems to find it difficult to believe laws have a place in establishing rights for people, but nevertheless even he is in favour of the principle set out in this bill, namely that workers should have two weeks' holidays with pay after one year's service.
That accounts for eight of the hon. members who have spoken. There is only one other, and of course he is a rather important person. I refer to the Minister of Labour. He did not indicate that he could support the bill. He did not say he was against it nor that he was going to vote against it, but he said that at the moment at any rate he could not bring himself to support it. If the house will vote in accordance with the views which have been expressed by the nine members who have spoken there is no doubt as to the result. I certainly hope that will be the case.
I am most grateful, not only to those on this side of the house in the three opposition parties who have spoken in support of the bill but for the attention given to it by the Minister of Labour. I am of course pleased with the support which has been indicated by the hon. member for Vancouver South.
In summing up, since it is hardly necessary to do anything by way of reply in view of the fact that most of the speeches have been favourable to the bill, I might repeat just one or two facts which were given earlier in the debate. It is correct to say that there is legislation regarding annual vacations with pay on the statute books of six provinces, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. Incidentally, using the formula we have had occasion to discuss yesterday and today under another heading, those six provinces represent a majority of the provinces and also a majority of the Canadian people. It seems to be pretty well indicated that this principle is accepted in this country.
However, as far as those six provinces are concerned, only two of them have legislation which provides that there shall be two weeks'
vacation with pay after one year's service, those two being British Columbia and Saskatchewan. The other four provinces provide for one week's holidays with pay after one year's service. Some of them provide for a greater length of holidays after more years of service. These provincial laws relate to employees who come under provincial labour legislation, ancf do not touch the 400,000 who come under federal jurisdiction. This bill would deal with that group of 400,000 workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction.
Nevertheless, I think the point should be made that there is a tendency on the part of the provinces, particularly in the labour field, to pay attention to what the other provinces are doing and to what the federal government is doing. I think if a lead could be given by the federal parliament in this matter it would hasten the day when we would have legislation of this kind throughout Canada, so that all the workers of this country would have vacations with pay as a matter of right. This is a principle which the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo accepts; and I think even he will have to agree that that can be brought about only if we use the rule of law to establish the rights to which we believe our people are entitled. After all, laws are not just the negative things that he seems to think they are; laws are not just restrictive, laws are also positive in that they establish certain rights. That is what this law is. It is similar to the laws in some of the provinces which do establish the right of working people in this country to enjoy two weeks' holidays with pay after one year's service.
May I say to the hon. member for Bow River that I indicated on May 11 when I moved second reading that I would be happy to have this bill go to the committee on industrial relations. If it is given second reading I would move that that be done, rather than the usual motion of reference to committee of the whole house.
I should like to say just a brief word further with respect to the number of employees who would be affected by this bill, following along the exchange between the hon. member for Vancouver South and myself. I think we got it clear, basing our statements on the table put on the record on May 11 by the Minister of Labour, that approximately 47 per cent of the employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction now have, by virtue of collective agreements or for other reasons, two weeks' holidays with pay after one year's service. That leaves some 53 per cent who would gain if this bill became law.

Industrial Relations
It is true that in addition to the 47 per cent who have two weeks' holidays with pay after one year's service there is roughly another 2 per cent who have two weeks' holidays with pay after two years' service and there is another 44 per cent who get two weeks' holidays with pay after three years' service. If you add those three groups together you arrive at the 93 per cent indicated a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Vancouver South.
However, I think cognizance should be taken of the fact that even the 47 per cent of the employees under federal labour jurisdiction who enjoy two weeks' holidays with pay after one year's service includes three groups of workers who I think it would be fair to say are in preferred categories. Those three groups are air transport employees, bank employees including employees of the Bank of Canada, and employees in government enterprises not included in the preceding classifications. The employees in those three groups, as will be seen from the table on page 3837 of Hansard, enjoy two weeks' holidays with pay after one year's service to the extent of 100 per cent. When you deduct those employees from the total and consider the rest, that is all employees under federal labour jurisdiction except those in preferred occupations who enjoy this privilege 100 per cent, you find that so far as the rest of them are concerned -in other words, averaging those in railways, shipping, motor and all other transport, mining, manufacturing and so on-it works out to about 35 per cent of all the rest who enjoy the privilege of two weeks' holidays with pay after one year's service.
I believe the principle is gaining ground, t believe it is pretty well accepted in Canada that people should have reasonable holidays vith pay as a result of their contribution to the economy of this country. Nevertheless it is true that there are still a great many people who come under federal labour jurisdiction who need the improved benefits and protection provided by legislation such as this. So I hope the house will give approval to this bill so it can be sent to the industrial relations committee.
As I say, seven of the nine of those who have spoken say they are for it and the eighth member says he is in favour of the principle although not in favour of doing it by law. If the eight of us can just get the Minister of Labour on our side we will have won the day.
